sentences.text: Every public official eventually faces the same hard choice: whether to do what is realistic today or to aim for what would be best in principle.
Those who favor feasibility argue that leaders must work with the world as it is, not as they wish it to be, and that chasing perfect solutions only wastes time and public money.
The choice sounds simple, but it quietly shapes almost everything a government does.
There is real wisdom in this caution, but I believe officials should be guided first by their ideals, because ideals are what slowly expand the limits of what is feasible.
First, many goals that once seemed impossible later became ordinary, precisely because someone refused to accept the limits of their time.
The end of legalized slavery, the right of women to vote, and the idea that governments should protect public health were all dismissed as unrealistic when they were first proposed.
In each case, the people who pushed these reforms forward were guided by an ideal rather than by what seemed achievable at the moment.
If every leader had done only what was easy and popular, none of these changes would have happened, and we would still call them impossible today.
What looks feasible, in other words, is not fixed; it is shaped by the goals that determined leaders are willing to fight for over many years.
The boundary of the possible, then, is something leaders help to redraw, not a wall they are simply stuck behind.
Of course, ideals on their own are not enough, and here the warning behind the claim deserves respect.
A leader who refuses every imperfect law while waiting for a perfect one may, in the end, help no one at all.
A politician who blocks a useful health program because it does not yet cover everyone has chosen a clean conscience over real human benefit.
Genuine progress almost always arrives in small, imperfect steps rather than in a single perfect leap.
A leader who ignores feasibility entirely can do real damage, no matter how noble the goal that inspired the attempt.
Good intentions do not feed anyone if the plan behind them never actually works.
The wisest approach, therefore, is to treat ideals and feasibility as partners rather than rivals.
An official should hold a clear ideal as the destination and then use practical, feasible actions as the steps that gradually move society toward it.
A government that wants clean air, for example, may not be able to ban all pollution at once, but it can raise its standards year after year until the ideal is finally reached.
Each step is realistic on its own, yet together the steps carry society toward a goal that once looked impossible.
This is how real reform usually happens: a distant ideal pursued through a long sequence of achievable moves.
In conclusion, feasibility and ideals are not really opposites, because each one needs the other.
Ideals without feasibility remain dreams, while feasibility without ideals leads nowhere in particular, so the best officials aim at what is ideal while moving forward one feasible step at a time.
